igcse-0580-money-totals-and-change.description: Use unit prices and fixed charges to find a bill, check change and work with a simple budget.

sections.title: How do I build a total from a price list?
sections.label: Build a total
sections.intro: Start by deciding what the price is for. A price ‘each’ applies to every item. A single fee applies to the order as a whole.

blocks.html: Multiply each unit price by its quantity. Add the item costs and any fixed fee.

figure.alt: An item subtotal and a fixed charge both flow into the total bill.
figure.caption: Add the item subtotal and the single fixed charge.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Write a line for each cost. For instance, a reader buying three £2.45 notebooks with one £1.80 collection fee writes an item subtotal and a single fee.

A small order
ItemQuantityCharge
Notebooks3£2.45 each
Collection1£1.80 once

blocks.title: Work out a total with delivery
blocks.prompt: A photography club orders 3 mounts at £3.02 each. Delivery costs £1.96 for the whole order. Find the total cost.
blocks.hint: Work out the cost of the mounts first. Delivery is charged once for the order.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the price of one mount by 3. The mounts cost £9.06.

Add delivery once. The total is £11.02.

retry.feedback: The mounts are correct. Add the fixed delivery charge.
The delivery charge is for the whole order. Add it once.
There is more than one mount. Multiply the unit price by the quantity.

blocks.html: A fixed charge is counted once. Multiplying the charge by the quantity makes the total too large.

blocks.title: Find the change from a payment
blocks.prompt: A customer pays £20.00 in cash for 5 exercise books costing £2.25 each. How much change should the customer receive?
blocks.hint: Change is the payment minus the total cost. Calculate the whole purchase before subtracting.
blocks.solution:
Multiply £2.25 by 5 to find the total spent, £11.25.

Subtract that total from the cash handed over. The change is £8.75.

retry.feedback: That is the total paid for the books. Subtract it from the cash handed over.
Subtract the cost of all the books. You have counted only one.
Change is what remains after spending. Subtract the cost.

sections.title: Which amounts are added and which are subtracted?
sections.label: Check money out
sections.intro: A cash pot grows when money comes in. A purchase reduces what is left. A receipt can help you track the running balance.

blocks.html: For change use the cash handed over minus the total cost. For a pot, begin with the opening amount, add receipts and subtract payments.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: If the question asks what remains, check your answer against the amount available before you paid. It should be smaller unless money also came in.

blocks.title: Follow money paid in and out
blocks.prompt: A studio has £32.30 in its cash pot. It receives £17.47, then pays £7.64 for tape and £5.51 for labels. How much remains?
blocks.hint: Sort the amounts into money coming in and money being paid out.
blocks.solution:
Add money received to the opening amount. The pot now contains £49.77.

The two payments cost £13.15. Subtract both to give £36.62.

retry.feedback: The studio receives the income. Add it and subtract what the studio pays.
There are two payments. Subtract the cost of the labels too.
The opening amount was already in the pot. Include it.

blocks.html: Cash paid and goods bought are different amounts. Keep the cash payment separate from the bill until the subtraction for change.

blocks.title: Find the change from a payment
blocks.prompt: A customer pays £40.00 in cash for 2 exercise books costing £3.27 each. How much change should the customer receive?
blocks.hint: Change is the payment minus the total cost. Calculate the whole purchase before subtracting.
blocks.solution:
Multiply £3.27 by 2 to find the total spent, £6.54.

Subtract that total from the cash handed over. The change is £33.46.

retry.feedback: That is the total paid for the books. Subtract it from the cash handed over.
Subtract the cost of all the books. You have counted only one.
Change is what remains after spending. Subtract the cost.

sections.title: How many whole items fit the budget?
sections.label: Fit the budget
sections.intro: Allow for anything you must pay once before working out how many items will fit.

blocks.html: Set aside the fee. Divide what is left by the unit price. Use the greatest affordable whole number. Check the spending with that number.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: A quotient of 6.8 means six whole items fit. Work out what six cost and subtract the complete bill from the original budget.

blocks.title: Find what is left after the largest order
blocks.prompt: A craft club can spend £20.27 on identical reels. One reel costs £5.55. The shop charges £2.80 delivery once. How much of the budget remains after buying as many whole reels as possible?
blocks.hint: Remove the fixed delivery charge from the budget before finding how many reels you can buy.
blocks.solution:
Set aside delivery. The amount available for reels is £17.47.

Divide by the price per reel and take the whole number that fits. 3 reels cost £16.65.

Subtract that cost and the delivery charge from £20.27. This leaves £0.82.

retry.feedback: You still need to pay the fixed delivery charge.
That is the amount spent. The question asks how much remains.

blocks.html: Rounding up can buy an item that the budget cannot cover. Check that one more item would exceed the budget.

blocks.prompt: A studio has £35.45 in its cash pot. It receives £19.36, then pays £8.27 for tape and £5.93 for labels. How much remains?
blocks.hint: Sort the amounts into money coming in and money being paid out.
blocks.solution:
Add money received to the opening amount. The pot now contains £54.81.

The two payments cost £14.20. Subtract both to give £40.61.

retry.feedback: The studio receives the income. Add it and subtract what the studio pays.
There are two payments. Subtract the cost of the labels too.
The opening amount was already in the pot. Include it.

blocks.html: Label the subtotal, the bill and the change in your working. Write two digits after the point for pounds and pence.

revision.body:
How do I build a total from a price list?

Multiply each unit price by its quantity. Add the item costs and any fixed fee.

Write a line for each cost. For instance, a reader buying three £2.45 notebooks with one £1.80 collection fee writes an item subtotal and a single fee.

Which amounts are added and which are subtracted?

For change use the cash handed over minus the total cost. For a pot, begin with the opening amount, add receipts and subtract payments.

If the question asks what remains, check your answer against the amount available before you paid. It should be smaller unless money also came in.

How many whole items fit the budget?

Set aside the fee. Divide what is left by the unit price. Use the greatest affordable whole number. Check the spending with that number.

A quotient of 6.8 means six whole items fit. Work out what six cost and subtract the complete bill from the original budget.

Quick worked example

A photography club orders 4 mounts at £3.44 each. Delivery costs £2.02 for the whole order. Find the total cost.

Multiply the price of one mount by 4. The mounts cost £13.76.

Add delivery once. The total is £15.78.
revision.checks:
• Have I counted each item and each fixed charge correctly?
  • Does the question ask for the cost or for the money left?
  • Is the answer in pounds and pence?
revision.examTip: Label the subtotal, the bill and the change in your working. Write two digits after the point for pounds and pence.

igcse-0580-money-exchange-rates.description: Read an exchange quote, choose the operation for each direction and compare prices in a common currency.

sections.title: When do I multiply by the rate?
sections.label: From the one
sections.intro: The quote £1 = €1.23 tells you what one pound buys. Check which currency is on the one side of the quote.

blocks.html: Starting from the quoted one-unit currency, multiply by the amount on the other side. For £1 = €1.23, multiply pounds by 1.23 to find euros.

figure.alt: Pounds and euros with a right-pointing arrow for multiplication and a left-pointing arrow for division, for a quote given in euros per pound.
figure.caption: With a quote of euros per pound, multiply pounds to get euros. Divide euros to get pounds.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Test your operation on one pound first. It must produce €1.23. Then scale up to the amount in the question.

blocks.title: Exchange pounds for euros
blocks.prompt: At a counter, £1 buys €1.31. An organiser changes £268 into euros. How many euros does the organiser receive?
blocks.hint: Find the value in euros of one pound, then scale to the pounds given.
blocks.solution:
For every pound the organiser receives €1.31. Multiply the pounds by \(1.31\).

\(268\times 1.31\) gives €351.08.

retry.feedback: The rate gives euros for one pound. Multiply when you start with pounds.
The number of euros for one pound is a multiplier, not an added charge.

blocks.html: Write the currency after every value. The number alone cannot tell you which direction the calculation went.

blocks.title: Use a quote written per euro
blocks.prompt: A bureau quotes €1 = £0.84. An exhibitor exchanges €267 for pounds. How many pounds does the exhibitor receive?
blocks.hint: Begin from the quote as written. Each euro buys the given amount in pounds.
blocks.solution:
This quote starts with one euro. So each euro buys £0.84.

Multiply the euros by \(0.84\). The exhibitor receives £224.28.

retry.feedback: The rate is pounds per euro, so multiply the euros. Dividing would undo that conversion.

sections.title: How do I go back the other way?
sections.label: Back to the one
sections.intro: If you already have euros, ask how many groups of the quoted euro amount you can make.

blocks.html: From euros back to pounds, undo the previous multiplication. Divide the euro amount by the euros per pound.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: If £1 buys more than €1, the number of pounds will be smaller than the number of euros for the same amount of money. Check the size and write the requested precision.

blocks.title: Exchange euros for pounds
blocks.prompt: A collector has €418. Use the exchange rate £1 = €1.48. Calculate the value in pounds to the nearest penny.
blocks.hint: Ask how many groups of the quoted euro amount are in the given total.
blocks.solution:
One pound uses €1.48. Divide the euros by euros per pound.

The calculation is \(418\div 1.48\). Round that result to get £282.43.

retry.feedback: This starts with euros. To undo the euros-per-pound multiplication, divide by the rate.
Use the quote as a conversion factor. Divide rather than subtracting the quote.
The question asks for the nearest penny. Return to the full calculation and round to two decimal places.

blocks.html: Turning around in the quote changes the operation. Test it using the two amounts printed in the quote.

blocks.title: Exchange pounds for euros
blocks.prompt: At a counter, £1 buys €1.52. An organiser changes £331 into euros. How many euros does the organiser receive?
blocks.hint: Find the value in euros of one pound, then scale to the pounds given.
blocks.solution:
For every pound the organiser receives €1.52. Multiply the pounds by \(1.52\).

\(331\times 1.52\) gives €503.12.

retry.feedback: The rate gives euros for one pound. Multiply when you start with pounds.
The number of euros for one pound is a multiplier, not an added charge.

sections.title: How do I handle fees and compare prices?
sections.label: Fees and comparisons
sections.intro: Work out which currency each fee is charged in and when it applies. Express both prices in one currency before deciding which is cheaper.

blocks.html: For a fee deducted from the cash handed over, reduce that amount first. Then convert what remains.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: When comparing prices, put both in the currency requested in the question. Subtract the lower full value from the higher full value, then round the difference.

blocks.title: Deduct the fee before exchanging
blocks.prompt: A customer hands over £279 to buy euros. The bureau first keeps a fee of £3.07. It converts the remaining pounds at £1 = €1.12. How many euros does the customer receive to the nearest cent?
blocks.hint: The fee is in pounds. Deduct it while the amount is still in pounds.
blocks.solution:
Take the fee from the pounds. That leaves £275.93 for the exchange.

Multiply this by \(1.12\) euros per pound. The customer receives €309.04 after rounding.

retry.feedback: Subtracting the pound fee after conversion treats the fee as euros.
The bureau keeps its fee first. Convert the balance in pounds only.
You took the fee in the correct currency. Multiply to find the euros received.

blocks.html: The fee is an amount of money with a unit. Subtract it from an amount in that same currency.

blocks.title: Compare two prices in one currency
blocks.prompt: A case costs £48.40 from one seller and €55.44 from another. Use £1 = €1.16 and ignore fees. How much less does the cheaper case cost, in pounds to the nearest penny?
blocks.hint: Before subtracting, express both prices in pounds.
blocks.solution:
Convert €55.44 to pounds by dividing by \(1.16\). Keep the full value for the subtraction.

The price in euros is cheaper. Subtract the lower value in pounds from the higher one. The difference is £0.61.

retry.feedback: One price is in pounds and one is in euros. Convert to the same currency first.
That is the euro price in pounds. Subtract to find the difference.

blocks.html: Write the quote first and label both currencies. Keep calculator digits until the final amount or difference.

igcse-0580-money-simple-interest.description: Use the starting deposit and an annual rate to work out simple interest, the ending balance or a missing deposit.

sections.title: Why is the interest the same each year?
sections.label: One year first
sections.intro: In a simple-interest account the calculation uses the starting deposit every year. The amount earned in year one is repeated in year two.

blocks.html: Work out one year's interest first. A 3.6% rate means 3.6 out of every 100 pounds of the starting deposit per year.

figure.alt: The same initial deposit supplies the amount on which interest is calculated in each of two years.
figure.caption: Simple interest uses the same original deposit again in year two.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: For principal \(P\), annual rate \(r\) written as a decimal and time \(t\) in years, interest is \(I=Prt\). Add the principal only if asked for the balance.

blocks.title: Calculate simple interest earned
blocks.prompt: A school association saves £3945 at \(5.1\)% simple interest per year. Find the interest it earns in 2 years to the nearest penny.
blocks.hint: Work out interest on the original deposit. The same amount is earned each year.
blocks.solution:
Interest for one year is \(5.1\)% of £3945, which is \(201.195\) pounds. Keep this value for the next step.

Multiply that same annual amount by 2. The interest is £402.39.

retry.feedback: That is the balance. Report only the interest.
That is one year of interest. Multiply by the full number of years.
The account pays simple interest. It pays the same amount each year.

blocks.html: A balance and interest earned answer different questions. Use the wording of the final line to decide which to give.

blocks.title: Find the final balance with simple interest
blocks.prompt: A community workshop deposits £4045 at \(5.5\)% simple interest per year. Calculate the balance after 6 years to the nearest penny.
blocks.hint: The balance includes the starting amount and the interest.
blocks.solution:
The deposit earns \(222.475\) pounds per year. In 6 years it earns \(1334.85\) pounds.

Add the whole amount earned to the original deposit. The balance is £5379.85.

retry.feedback: You found the interest. Add it to the principal for the balance.
This balance is for one year. Include the full term.
The account pays simple interest. Apply the rate to the starting amount each year.

sections.title: How do I use a term given in months?
sections.label: Match the time unit
sections.intro: If the question says simple interest is paid proportionally for part of a year, work with the same time unit as the rate.

blocks.html: For an annual rate, the time in years is \(\dfrac{\text{months}}{12}\). For instance, 18 months is \(\frac{18}{12}=1.5\) years.

revision.body:
Why is the interest the same each year?

Work out one year's interest first. A 3.6% rate means 3.6 out of every 100 pounds of the starting deposit per year.

For principal \(P\), annual rate \(r\) written as a decimal and time \(t\) in years, interest is \(I=Prt\). Add the principal only if asked for the balance.

How do I use a term given in months?

For an annual rate, the time in years is \(\dfrac{\text{months}}{12}\). For instance, 18 months is \(\frac{18}{12}=1.5\) years.

Multiply one year's interest by the fraction or decimal number of years. Keep the full values until the final answer.

How can I recover the starting deposit?

Over the full term, the interest is \(rt\) times the starting deposit. Use \(P=\dfrac{I}{rt}\) if the question gives the interest itself.

Multiply your proposed deposit by the annual decimal rate and the number of years. You should recover the stated interest.

Quick worked example

A school association saves £745 at \(4.1\)% simple interest per year. Find the interest it earns in 4 years to the nearest penny.

Interest for one year is \(4.1\)% of £745, which is \(30.545\) pounds. Keep this value for the next step.

Multiply that same annual amount by 4. The interest is £122.18.
